The numbers (commit 6ce3696, 2026-03-10) were measured on code that PR #19 (2026-09-22) later fixed for scoring bugs, which also keeps it at C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark run. The README builds with `zig build --release=fast` (optional -Dflto=true) and now requires Zig 0.16.x, but the benchmark lines date from commit 6ce3696 (2026-03-10), before the 2026-04-22 move to Zig 0.16.
corrections.caveats: Off the category baselines: a perceptual quality metric compared with the Python ColorVideoVDP reference, not a codec. First-party single-clip benchmark (302 frames of 360p, fm360p.y4m not shipped, no benchmark script in the repo). The reference ran as 'cvvdp (multithreaded)' with PyTorch version and device unstated; 777G cycles over 19.1 s is about 40G cycles/s, consistent with several CPU cores busy (derived from page data), and its wall time includes Python/PyTorch start-up and video decoding, which the README does not separate. Output equivalence is not shown in the README: PR #19 ('vship parity fixes', 2026-09-22) fixed an inverse-RFFT initialization bug that erased half of each temporal kernel, CSF interpolation weights, RGB-to-XYZ coefficients and Y4M colour range, which had produced errors of 0.155064 and 0.220898 JOD against FFVship on two clips (about 0.000002 after the fix). The README timings (2026-03-10) were measured on the pre-fix code; the PR reports only 1-2% runtime change from the fix, and a 2026-07-13 commit claims about 20% faster CSF weighting, so current timings differ. Parity is checked against Vship/FFVship, not directly against the Python cvvdp baseline. The 8-thread run executes 21.6% more instructions than the reference. The README's '28% faster' and '221% faster' are wall-time ratios 19.1/14.9 = 1.28x and 19.1/5.94 = 3.22x. Derived from Vship (MIT). C core with Zig build and CLI; GitHub's language bar was not visible.

tier_reason: The repo (README, qoa.h, qoaconv.c, Makefile, issues) has no comparison numbers; the only numbers are the author's 2023 blog benchmark table (phoboslab.org, blocked here) seen through search snippets, which name the file, CPU (i7-6700K) and single-threaded ffmpeg default settings but no QOA build flags or harness. Snippet-only first-party numbers cap it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (author's post 'QOA Benchmark Results and File Format Specification', blocked here): on a 2 h 43 min (9807 s, 1650 MB) 44.1 kHz stereo track, single-threaded on an i7-6700K, QOA encode 25.752 s and decode 2.996 s; Opus via ffmpeg default settings encode 315.232 s and decode 20.410 s (116 MB file); MP3 via ffmpeg encode 146.223 s and decode 9.631 s (149 MB); Vorbis via ffmpeg decode 8.732 s. Versus Opus 12.2x encode and 6.8x decode; versus MP3 5.7x encode and 3.2x decode (derived from snippet data). The author's informal summary: 'QOA encodes 10x faster and decodes 7x faster than Opus'. The repo README, qoa.h and issues contain no numbers.
corrections.workload: Single-threaded encode and decode of one 2 h 43 min 44.1 kHz stereo film soundtrack (author's 2023 blog benchmark), QOA's reference implementation versus Opus, MP3 and Vorbis run through the ffmpeg CLI at ffmpeg's default settings with output to /dev/null.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark. The repo Makefile builds qoaconv with CC ?= gcc and -std=c99 -O3.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-6700K, single-threaded (from search snippets of the author's blog post)
corrections.caveats: Numbers come only from search-result snippets of the author's 2023 blog post (phoboslab.org, qoaformat.org and news.ycombinator.com are blocked here); the repo has no benchmark harness (qoaconv only prints clock() timings for its own decode/encode). Different work: QOA is a fixed-rate time-domain codec at 3.2 bits per sample (about 280 kbit/s for 44.1 kHz stereo, roughly 330 MB here, derived from qoa.h), while Opus at ffmpeg's default bitrate produced 116 MB (about 95-99 kbit/s, derived from snippet data) using a transform codec with psychoacoustic analysis, so the speed gap compares different bitrates and quality targets. Opus and MP3 timings include ffmpeg CLI overhead (the author notes ffmpeg's considerable overhead) and, for Opus, resampling 44.1 kHz to 48 kHz. The code has changed since 2023 (2026 fixes for out-of-bounds access and integer wrap-around in decoding). The README warns the implementation has not been fuzzed and must not be used with untrusted input. A Hacker News commenter argues QOA is slower than ADPCM and compresses less than MP3. Ports (qoa-fu, qoaudio, goqoa, qoa-format and others) are reimplementations of the same format.

notes: Kept at C under the snippet-only rule: the blog URL came from search results and could not be opened, so page_compares_against_baseline and numbers_found_on_page are null; two separate snippets gave a consistent table. Notable (985 stars, 57 forks, used by Godot 4.3, raylib, SerenityOS); MIT and last commit 2026-09-27 confirmed on github.com.

tier_reason: The README low-delay tables give xin26x and x265 FPS and PSNR with full command lines, matching the record (2.60x, 4.69x, 4.40x, 2.35x derived from page data), but no CPU, compiler, flags or x265 build for these runs, the sequences are not in the repo, and the measured HEVC encoder ships only as prebuilt binaries, so it is first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for either benchmarked binary. The HEVC encoder and shared core are prebuilt Windows static libraries (h26x_core.lib, h265_core.lib, h265_enc.lib) of unknown compiler and flags; CMakeLists.txt adds -W4 /arch:AVX and -Oi -GL (MSVC release) only for the parts built from source. Commands: xin26x_test.exe -a 0 -I 0 --wpp 0 --thread 1 --preset 0 (preset 3 for BasketballDrive) --bframes 0 (-s 1 for sc_desktop); x265.exe --preset fast -I -1 --pools 1 --bframes 0 --frame-threads 0 --no-wpp --tune psnr. The x265 2020/12/25 version is stated only for the offline BD-rate table.
corrections.caveats: The measured HEVC encoder is closed: h26x_core/h26x_core.lib, h265_core/h265_core.lib and h265_encoder/h265_enc.lib are prebuilt Windows static libraries that CMakeLists.txt imports as STATIC IMPORTED, with no HEVC source in the repo (only the VVC h266_*, AV1-intra h265p_*, API and app code have source under AGPL-3.0), so the fast code cannot be read, audited or rebuilt for other platforms; open issue #15 (2023) reports a Visual Studio build that produces an executable that does nothing and doubts all code is included, and Linux build issues #10/#12 exist. First-party table only: CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated, and the test sequences are not in the repo (only a Google Drive link to xin26x bitstreams). xin26x presets differ per sequence (preset 3 for BasketballDrive, preset 0 elsewhere) against x265 --preset fast, which is not x265's fastest preset (ultrafast to faster are quicker), so the gap is not at matched effort; PSNR is matched within 0.04 dB at equal ABR bitrate for the three natural sequences (PSNR only, no BD-rate for the low-delay runs). The sc_desktop row is not like for like (xin26x's screen-content tool -s 1, PSNR 40.082 versus 29.817). x265 --frame-threads 0 is its auto setting, which with --pools 1 should resolve to one frame thread; CPU utilisation is not reported. The README says lookahead and cu-tree are enabled in both. x86 AVX2 only. The repo dates to 2020 (issue #1, 2020-08-19; 215 commits); the first commits page only reaches back to 2026-04-28.

notes: Confirmed at C with usability corrected to mixed: the benchmarked HEVC encoder and shared core are binary-only .lib files, which matters more for this catalog than the speed claim. License AGPL-3.0 (LICENSE file), 108 stars, 10 forks, last commit 2026-08-26 confirmed via github.com pages.
